summary: Gives more detail on how policy fits into the Path Computation Element architecture, and proposes using the Policy Core Information Model as a framework for path computation policy. It includes example scenarios. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: A trip planner may need rules like never use this road or prefer cheap routes. This memo describes how to attach such rules to the planner.

questions: how to control path computation decisions
what is a policy decision point
subtitle: Rules for controlling how the network picks paths for traffic.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a way to shape how the Path Computation Element picks routes for traffic, applying business rules and constraints that simple algorithms do not capture.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses the Policy Core Information Model as a framework, allowing operators to define policies that guide path computation decisions. Policies can be applied at path computation clients (PCCs) or path computation elements (PCEs) to control constraints, optimization criteria, and constraint relaxation.
tldr.outcome: This framework enables operators to dynamically introduce new path computation capabilities without requiring changes to protocols or widespread software upgrades, by allowing new constraints and objectives to be expressed as policies.

today: RFC 5394 is an Informational RFC that provides guidance on incorporating policy into PCE architectures. The policy framework it describes continues to be used in MPLS-TE and GMPLS networks where path computation is centralized. Later standards documents have built on this framework.

sections.title: Introduction to Policy-Based Path Computation
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) architecture lets network operators query a separate system to find the best route for traffic, instead of computing routes locally at each router. This RFC shows how to add policy rules to path computation so that operators can control how routes are selected.

Path computation decisions are governed by constraints (for example, find a path with at least 10 Mbps available bandwidth) and objectives (for example, minimize cost). Without policies, these must be hard-coded. Policies allow operators to define complex rules on the fly, such as: if the destination is in the customer network, prefer low-cost paths; if the destination is mission-critical, find two disjoint paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Policies are like instructions an operator can write without changing the software: use this path for customers, avoid that link for backups, prefer cheap routes when possible.

sections.title: Why Policies Matter in Path Computation
sections.content:
Network operators face a fundamental problem: they need flexibility to shape path computation to match business and operational needs, but different services may have very different requirements. A video streaming service might need high bandwidth and low delay, while a backup service might accept any path with minimum cost. Different services may also need different constraint relaxation strategies: one service might accept a path with slightly lower bandwidth, while another rejects such paths entirely.

Historically, flexibility came from upgrading router software. With the PCE architecture, adding new capabilities becomes harder because PCCs and PCEs must use standardized discovery and communication protocols. If a PCE gains a new constraint (like optical impairment awareness), the PCC must know about it, PCE discovery protocols must advertise it, and both may need upgrades. Policies solve this by encoding constraints and objectives as interpretable rules that can be updated and distributed without changing core protocols.

The RFC presents four scenarios: operators can use policies to configure pre-computed paths per service, to select which transit domain routes traffic through in a multi-domain network, to provide constraints based on service type without requiring the PCC to understand every constraint type, and to perform advanced load balancing based on offered traffic load rather than just topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Without policies, adding a new routing rule requires updating software on many routers. With policies, an operator can write the rule once and apply it everywhere, making the network much more flexible.

sections.title: The Policy-Enabled PCE Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture introduces two key new components at both the PCC and PCE sides: a Policy Decision Point (PDP) that retrieves policies from a repository and a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that applies those policies to guide computation. At the PCE, the PCE-PDP retrieves policies and the PCE-PEP uses them to decide which algorithm to apply, whether to ask other PCEs for help, and how to handle the request. At the PCC, the PCC-PDP retrieves policies and the PCC-PEP uses them to select which PCE to query and what constraints to request.

Policy repositories store policies centrally and can be shared between PCCs and PCEs within a domain, or kept separate for different domains. Policies themselves are expressed using the Policy Core Information Model (PCIM), a vendor-independent framework that defines policy structures (rules, conditions, actions) using object-oriented classes. The RFC does not specify the exact PCIM definitions for path computation; that is left to a separate document.

The architecture is flexible about deployment: operators can apply policies at PCCs, at PCEs, or at both. Some policy types might be applied at the PCC (such as selecting which PCE to use), while others are applied at the PCE (such as domain-specific policies). In some networks, all policy logic runs at the PCE and the PCC simply sends service information to be interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCE and PCC each have a policy rule book that they read from a shared policy library. When a request arrives, they look up the relevant rules and apply them to make decisions about routing.

sections.title: How Policies Guide Path Computation
sections.content:
When a path computation request arrives, the PCE-PEP validates it and applies request-specific policies found within the request itself, as well as client-specific, user-specific, and domain-specific policies from the policy repository. The result is a decision on whether to satisfy, reject, or dismiss the request, which constraints to honor, which PCE to ask for help if needed, and whether to perform local computation.

The flow typically works as follows: First, the PCC receives a service request (for example, an MPLS setup message). The PCC applies service-specific policies to determine what constraints and optimization criteria are needed. The PCC then applies server-specific policies to select which PCE to contact, possibly modifying the request to fit the PCE's capabilities. The resulting path computation request is sent to the PCE.

At the PCE, the request is processed by applying request-specific policies found in the request, as well as local policies. The PCE-PEP may decide to satisfy the request locally, ask other PCEs for help (possibly modifying the request per requester-specific policies), or deny the request. A successful computation returns the computed path(s) and may include additional policy information describing which constraints were honored, which were relaxed, and how.
sections.plainLanguage: When the PCC wants a path, it writes down the service type and which constraints it needs, based on its policy rules. The PCE reads those rules and its own rules, then decides which algorithm to use and whether to ask other PCEs for help.

sections.title: Discovering and Introducing New Capabilities
sections.content:
A key benefit of the policy framework is that new constraints can be introduced without upgrading PCE-PCC communication protocols or requiring all PCEs to support them. When a PCE gains a new capability (for example, support for an optical impairment constraint), one or more new policies are installed in the PCE policy repository. These policies define the constraint, its relaxation strategy, and how it applies to which services.

In the single-repository case, PDPs at both PCCs and PCEs retrieve the new policies automatically. PCC-PDPs then instruct PCC-PEPs to include the new policy information in requests for matching service types. PCE-PDPs provide the new policies to the PCE-PEP, which applies them when processing requests. Because the new policies are carried as opaque policy objects in the PCE communication protocol, the protocol itself does not need to change. PCCs and PCEs that do not understand a new policy can safely ignore it, while those that do can apply it.

This approach also naturally solves the PCE capability discovery problem: once a policy is installed in a shared repository, it becomes available to all users without explicit capability advertisement.
sections.plainLanguage: If the PCE learns to handle a new constraint, the operator just adds a policy rule to the shared library. All PCCs will start using it automatically, without any protocol changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that policy-enabled path computation introduces new security concerns beyond those in the base PCE architecture. Policy repositories must be protected from unauthorized access. Policy information must be protected when retrieved from repositories and transported between PDPs and PEPs. Interception of policy-related information in path computation requests and responses must be prevented, and impersonation of user and client identities must be blocked.

Additionally, falsification of policy information or misrepresentation of PCE capabilities could allow an attacker to redirect traffic or deny service. The RFC notes that PCE solutions are expected to address these security issues in detail, using authentication, authorization, and integrity protection mechanisms appropriate to their deployment context.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy rules are sensitive: if someone changes them without permission, they can trick the network into sending traffic the wrong way. So all policy information needs to be encrypted and authenticated.
